title: Teaching Team Members to Care About Customers and Clients
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that caring about customers can't be commanded directly -- it has to be built through curiosity. The author explains that leaders who simply instruct people to 'care more' get compliance theater rather than real engagement. Instead, the recommended method is to interrogate what a team member actually knows about a specific customer's background, interests, and life. The article frames curiosity and caring as inseparable, so building one habit naturally builds the other. It closes by noting that team members being quizzed this way rarely realize they are being trained, which lowers their resistance to the lesson.
points: Caring can't be taught by instruction alone; it has to be demonstrated through curiosity about specific people.
Leaders should ask pointed questions about individual customers' backstories, passions, and habits rather than accept vague claims of caring.
When team members can't answer detailed questions about a customer, the gap in their engagement becomes self-evident.
Repeated questioning builds curiosity indirectly, and curiosity in turn deepens genuine care over time.
quotes: The key is to understand that caring, curiosity and genuine interest are siblings that can’t be separated.
Instead, good leaders ask for proof. And the proof is in what they know about specific customers and clients, not in what they are instructed to do.
They ask for the customer’s backstory, where they came from, where they have lived, and how they grew up in the world.
When team members can’t answer these and other questions that reflect an understanding of specific customers and clients, the point is loudly made.
Team members who are peppered with questions about their customers don’t even know that they are being taught.
In fact, it is almost impossible to be curious without an elevated sense of caring.
